questions.question_text: For $f(x)=x^2$, what is the gradient of the secant line passing through $P(4, 16)$ and $Q(4.2, 17.64)$, where $h=0.2$?

options.why: Calculated the exact tangent gradient instead of the secant line gradient for $h=0.2$.
Computed the change in $y$ ($\Delta y = 1.64$) without dividing by $h=0.2$.
Divided the change in $y$ by $0.4$ instead of the horizontal step $h=0.2$.

questions.question_text: For $f(x)=x^2$, find the gradient of the secant line joining $P(-2, 4)$ and $Q(-1.9, 3.61)$, where $h=0.1$.

options.why: Stated the exact limit value instead of evaluating the secant line gradient at $h=0.1$.
Subtracted $h$ from the gradient instead of adding $h$ to $-4$.
Omitted the negative sign on the change in $y$.

questions.question_text:
The table below shows secant gradients $\dfrac{f(3+h)-f(3)}{h}$ for $f(x)=x^3$.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline h & -0.001 & 0.001 & 0.01 & 0.1 \\\hline m_{\text{secant}} & 26.991 & 27.009 & 27.09 & 27.91 \\\hline\end{array}$
What is the estimated gradient of the tangent to $f(x)=x^3$ at $x=3$?

options.why: Selected the secant gradient for $h=0.001$ rather than the limiting value as $h\to 0$.
Evaluated $3^2=9$ instead of multiplying by the power rule factor $3$.
Selected the first value in the table at $h=0.1$ instead of taking the limit as $h\to 0$.

questions.question_text:
The table below shows difference quotients for $f(x)=x^4$ at $x=-1$.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}\hline h & -0.001 & 0.001 & 0.01 \\\hline m_{\text{secant}} & -4.006 & -3.994 & -3.9404 \\\hline\end{array}$
What is the estimated value of $f'(-1)$?

options.why: Read off the secant gradient at the largest step size $h=0.01$ instead of finding the limit as $h\to 0$.
Read off the value at $h=0.001$ without inferring the integer limit.
Confused the $x$-coordinate with the gradient limit.

questions.question_text: On a smooth curve $y=f(x)$, what happens geometrically to the secant line through $P(c, f(c))$ and $Q(c+h, f(c+h))$ as $h\to 0$?

options.text: The secant line rotates to become the tangent line at $P$.
The secant line becomes a horizontal line through $P$.
options.why: Assumed the gradient approaches zero regardless of the curve's slope.

options.text: The secant line becomes perpendicular to the curve at $P$.
options.why: Confused the tangent line with the normal line.

options.text: The secant line disappears because $h=0$ cannot exist.
options.why: Confused an algebraic division by zero with the geometric limit of a rotating line.

questions.solution_text:
As $h\to 0$, $Q$ approaches $P$ along the curve.
The secant line rotates to become the tangent line at $P$.

questions.question_text: For any function $f(x)$, what does the expression $\dfrac{f(5+h)-f(5)}{h}$ represent when $h \neq 0$?

options.text: The gradient of the secant line passing through $(5, f(5))$ and $(5+h, f(5+h))$.
The exact gradient of the tangent line at $x=5$.
options.why: The expression gives the exact tangent gradient only in the limit as $h\to 0$, not for non-zero $h$.

options.text: The instantaneous rate of change of $f(x)$ at $x=5+h$.
options.why: The difference quotient gives an average rate of change between two points, not the instantaneous rate at $5+h$.

options.text: The vertical distance between the two points on the curve.
options.why: The expression is the ratio of vertical change to horizontal change, not vertical distance alone.

questions.solution_text: The difference quotient $\dfrac{f(5+h)-f(5)}{h}$ represents the gradient of the secant line between $(5, f(5))$ and $(5+h, f(5+h))$.

questions.question_text:
For $f(x)=x^2$ at $x=6$, the difference quotient simplifies to $\dfrac{(6+h)^2-36}{h}=12+h$.
Evaluate this for $h=0.02$ and state the estimated tangent gradient.

options.text: Secant gradient is $12.02$, approaching tangent gradient $12$.
Secant gradient is $12.02$, approaching tangent gradient $6$.
options.why: Evaluated $12+0.02=12.02$ correctly but then reported the $x$-coordinate $6$ as the limiting tangent gradient instead of the value $12+h$ approaches.

options.text: Secant gradient is $12.2$, approaching tangent gradient $12$.
options.why: Place-value slip when adding the decimal: wrote $12+0.02$ as $12.2$ instead of $12.02$, aligning the $2$ in the tenths column rather than the hundredths column.

options.text: Secant gradient is $12.2$, approaching tangent gradient $6$.
options.why: Made both slips: added $12+0.02$ as $12.2$ by lining the $2$ up in the tenths column, and then quoted the $x$-coordinate $6$ as the limiting gradient.

questions.question_text:
For $f(x)=3x^2$ at $x=1$, the difference quotient simplifies to $6+3h$.
What is the secant gradient for $h=0.05$ and the estimated instantaneous gradient as $h\to 0$?

options.text: Secant gradient is $6.15$; estimated instantaneous gradient is $6$.
Secant gradient is $6.15$; estimated instantaneous gradient is $3$.
options.why: Computed $6+3(0.05)=6.15$ correctly but then quoted the leading coefficient $3$ of $3x^2$ as the limiting gradient instead of the constant term $6$ that $6+3h$ approaches.

options.text: Secant gradient is $6.5$; estimated instantaneous gradient is $6$.
options.why: Multiplied $3\times 0.05$ as $0.5$ instead of $0.15$, losing a decimal place in the product, giving $6+0.5=6.5$.

options.text: Secant gradient is $6.5$; estimated instantaneous gradient is $3$.
options.why: Made both slips: took $3\times 0.05$ to be $0.5$ rather than $0.15$, and reported the leading coefficient $3$ as the limiting gradient.

questions.question_text:
A sequence of difference quotients for $f(x)=x^3$ at $x=c$ (where $c>0$) approaches $48$ as $h\to 0$.
Given that the limiting gradient is $3c^2=48$, what is $c$?

options.why: Found $c^2=16$ but forgot to take the square root to solve for $c$.
Calculated $48/(3\times 8)=2$ incorrectly instead of solving $3c^2=48$.
Divided $48$ by $6$ instead of solving $3c^2=48$.
